problem:
Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2t-4,\,{p}_{2}(t)=2-t,\,{p}_{3}(t)=1-t.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(1)q(1)+p(2)q(2),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

choices.value: None of the statements is true

activity_context.topic_title: Orthogonal Sets in Inner Product Spaces

feedback.problem:
Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

- ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
- $S={{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ differentiating we have $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{2}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
